sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel

In Excel's A1 notation, letters identify columns and numbers identify rows. When a formula is copied or filled, a relative reference preserves its offset from the formula cell: its row and column adjust with the copy displacement. A dollar sign fixes the component immediately following it. An absolute reference fixes both components; a mixed reference fixes only its column or only its row. Each reference in a formula follows its own anchors. These are copying/filling rules for ordinary cell references; cutting or moving cells, structural edits and structured table references are outside this summary.

question.prompt: A sales summary has regions in B2:E2 (North, South, East, West) and quarters in A3:A6 (Q1-Q4). Cell B3 should multiply the quarter factor in $A$1 by the regional target in $B$1, then fill across to E3 and down to E6. What should B3 contain?
question.topic: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 referenc

choiceFeedback.explanation: $A1 leaves the row of the quarter-factor cell relative, so copying down shifts it away from A1; the quarter factor must be fully fixed as $A$1.
B1 is fully relative so copying down shifts its row off row 1; $A$3 fully fixes the quarter row so copying down never picks up Q2–Q4.
$A$1 locks the shared quarter factor; B$1 keeps row 1 fixed while the column shifts right for each region; $A3 keeps column A fixed while the row shifts down for each quarter.
$B$1 fully fixes the regional target so every column uses North's value; A3 is fully relative so copying right shifts its column away from A, losing the quarter factors.

review.explanation: Each of the three operands needs its own anchor strategy: the shared constant needs full anchoring, the regional target needs its row fixed but column free, and the quarter factor needs its column fixed but row free.

question.prompt: A commission sheet has rates in A1:A5 and sales amounts in B1:F1. Cell B2 needs =A2*B1 so it can fill across to F2 and down to B5, always using the correct rate and amount. What should B2 contain?

$A locks column A for rates regardless of fill direction; $1 locks row 1 for amounts; both relative components adjust correctly as the formula fills.

question.prompt: A medical test for a rare disease (1 in 1000 prevalence) is 99% accurate: it correctly identifies 99% of sick people and 99% of healthy people. If you test positive, what is the approximate probability you actually have the disease?
question.topic: base rates and distinguishing a possible conclus

choiceFeedback.explanation: This ignores the base rate; with 1/1000 prevalence, false positives vastly outnumber true positives even with a 99% accurate test.
50% would require roughly equal true and false positives, implying ~50% prevalence, far above the stated 1/1000.
1% is near the raw base rate and ignores the updating power of a positive test result; Bayes' theorem gives ~9%.

review.explanation: Applying Bayes' theorem with a 1/1000 base rate shows that false positives (~999) swamp true positives (~99), yielding only ~9% posterior probability despite 99% test accuracy.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax food-web structure: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-1-ecology-of-ecosystems (Food Chains and Food Webs)

A food chain traces one route through feeding relationships; a food web includes intersecting routes. Primary consumers eat producers, while secondary consumers eat primary consumers. A species may feed at more than one trophic level, so its role depends on its feeding links. In the chapter's food-web convention, an arrow goes from food to the organism consuming it, showing the direction of energy transfer. A list of feeding links is not by itself a quantitative prediction of every population's response to a disturbance. Matter can be recycled through decomposers, while energy is lost from food-web transfers as heat.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax trophic production: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-2-energy-flow-through-ecosystems (Ecological Efficiency and Ecological Pyramids)

Trophic-level transfer efficiency compares production at a receiving trophic level with production at the preceding level, expressed as a percentage. Such efficiencies need not equal ten percent; use measured or explicitly stated values. Compare production over matching areas and time intervals. Successive trophic transfers leave less energy available along a chain. Standing biomass and energy production are different quantities: a small producer biomass can support a larger consumer biomass when producers replenish rapidly. An inverted biomass pyramid therefore does not establish an inverted energy-flow pyramid.

question.prompt: A pond ecosystem has phytoplankton with standing biomass 30 g/m² and annual production of 300 g/m²/year. Zooplankton have standing biomass 150 g/m². Transfer efficiency from phytoplankton to zooplankton is 25%. Which conclusion about zooplankton annual production is valid?
question.topic: Distinguish energy flow over time from a snapsho

choiceFeedback.explanation: Applying the stated 25% transfer efficiency to phytoplankton annual production (300 × 0.25 = 75 g/m²/year) gives this value correctly.
This equals the zooplankton standing biomass, not a production figure derived from transfer efficiency; it conflates biomass with annual production.
This would result from applying 25% to the phytoplankton standing biomass (30 × 1.25 ≠ 37.5; actually 30 × 1.25 = 37.5), incorrectly using standing biomass instead of annual production as the base.
This appears to apply a 10% default efficiency (300 × 0.025 = 7.5) rather than the explicitly stated 25%, ignoring the given transfer efficiency.

review.explanation: Transfer efficiency applies to annual production, not standing biomass. Multiplying phytoplankton annual production (300 g/m²/year) by the stated 25% efficiency yields 75 g/m²/year; the other choices misuse standing biomass or an unstated default efficiency.

question.prompt: A study finds that cities with more ice cream sales have higher drowning rates. A news headline claims 'Ice cream consumption increases drowning risk.' What is the most warranted conclusion?
choices: Drowning causes people to buy more ice cream
The correlation is probably a statistical fluke
A third factor (like hot weather) likely explains both patterns
question.topic: causal claims

review.answer: A third factor (like hot weather) likely explains both patterns

choiceFeedback.explanation: Correlation alone does not establish causation, and a plausible confounding variable makes a direct causal claim unwarranted.

choiceFeedback.choice: Drowning causes people to buy more ice cream
choiceFeedback.explanation: This reverses causality implausibly and is supported by neither the data nor any reasonable mechanism.

choiceFeedback.choice: The correlation is probably a statistical fluke
choiceFeedback.explanation: A well-known common cause (hot weather) explains the pattern; dismissing it as a fluke is less warranted than identifying the confounder.

choiceFeedback.choice: A third factor (like hot weather) likely explains both patterns
choiceFeedback.explanation: Hot weather independently increases both swimming activity and ice cream consumption, creating a spurious correlation — the most warranted conclusion.

review.explanation: A correlation between two variables is best explained by a common cause when a plausible confounder exists; hot weather drives both ice cream sales and drowning rates, making direct causation unwarranted.

question.prompt: Teams A, B, C and D completed 30 of 100, 21 of 60, 16 of 80 and 27 of 90 tasks respectively. Which team had the highest observed completion rate?
question.topic: Observed proportions

choiceFeedback.explanation: 30/100 = 30%, which is lower than Team B's 35%.
21/60 = 35%, the highest completion rate among all four teams.
16/80 = 20%, the lowest completion rate of the four teams.
27/90 = 30%, equal to Team A but below Team B's 35%.

review.explanation: Completion rate is tasks completed divided by tasks assigned. Converting each to a percentage: A=30%, B=35%, C=20%, D=30%, making Team B the clear leader.

question.prompt: A budget sheet has categories in A2:A10 and months in B1:M1. The formula in B2 divides category target (column N, same row) by 12 for monthly amount. B2 must fill across to M2 and down to M10. What should B2 contain?
question.topic: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 referenc

choiceFeedback.explanation: A fully relative reference shifts the column when filling right, so cells in columns C–M would reference O2, P2, … instead of staying in column N.
Locking the column with $ keeps the reference in column N for every column the formula fills into, while the row adjusts correctly when filling down.
Locking the row fixes the reference to row 2 for all rows, so filling down to rows 3–10 would still read from row 2 instead of the correct category row.
Locking both components fixes the reference to N2 for every cell in the table, ignoring both the column fill and the row fill.

review.explanation: The target value is always in column N but must follow the row when filling down, so only the column needs anchoring: =$N2/12.

sourceDocuments.name: Microsoft Excel reference rules: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel

In Excel's A1 notation, letters identify columns and numbers identify rows. When a formula is copied or filled, a relative reference preserves its offset from the formula cell: its row and column adjust with the copy displacement. A dollar sign fixes the component immediately following it. An absolute reference fixes both components; a mixed reference fixes only its column or only its row. Each reference in a formula follows its own anchors. These are copying/filling rules for ordinary cell references; cutting or moving cells, structural edits and structured table references are outside this summary.

question.prompt: A commission sheet has rates in A1:A5 and sales amounts in B1:F1. Cell B2 needs =A2*B1 so it can fill across to F2 and down to B5, always using the correct rate and amount. What should B2 contain?
question.topic: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 referenc

choiceFeedback.explanation: Both references are fully relative; filling right shifts the rate column away from A and filling down shifts the amount row away from row 1.
=$A2 locks column A so the rate stays in column A when filling right; B$1 locks row 1 so the amount stays in row 1 when filling down. Both adjust correctly in the other direction.
This locks the rate to row 2 and the amount to column B, which is the opposite of what is needed; filling down loses the correct rate and filling right loses the correct amount.
Locking both components of A2 means the rate never changes when filling down, so every row uses A2's rate instead of the row-specific rate.

review.explanation: To always reference the rate in column A (fixed column, variable row) and the amount in row 1 (fixed row, variable column), use mixed references =$A2 and B$1.

choiceFeedback.choice: Every eligible person preferred design A.

choiceFeedback.choice: No, some eligible people did not respond.

choiceFeedback.choice: The response counts do not establish whether everyone eligible responded.
choiceFeedback.explanation: Without knowing the total eligible population, the 80 response counts alone cannot determine whether participation was complete or partial.

review.explanation: The stem provides only response counts, not the size of the eligible population. Without that baseline, no conclusion about complete or incomplete participation is warranted.

question.prompt: A bag contains 30 red and 70 blue marbles. You draw one marble, note its color, return it, and draw again. Given that at least one draw was red, what is the probability both draws were red?
question.topic: Conditional probability

choiceFeedback.explanation: 51% is P(at least one red), the denominator of the conditional probability, not the conditional probability itself.
P(RR)=0.09, P(at least one R)=0.51; conditional probability=0.09/0.51≈17.6%≈18%.
9% is the unconditional P(both red)=0.3², ignoring the conditioning on at least one draw being red.
30% is the single-draw probability of red, not the conditional probability that both draws were red.

review.explanation: Conditioning on 'at least one red' restricts the sample space: divide P(both red)=0.09 by P(at least one red)=0.51 to get ≈18%.

question.prompt: A city has two hospitals: Large Hospital delivers 45 babies daily, Small Hospital delivers 15. Over one year, each hospital records the days when more than 60% of births were boys. Which hospital likely recorded more such days?
choices: Cannot be determined from the information given
question.topic: sampling

choiceFeedback.explanation: Larger daily samples produce proportions closer to the true 50%, making extreme deviations like >60% boys less frequent.
The hospitals' very different daily volumes (45 vs 15) produce substantially different variability, so outcomes cannot be equally frequent.

choiceFeedback.choice: Cannot be determined from the information given
choiceFeedback.explanation: Sampling theory directly predicts smaller samples show more extreme proportions; the given information is sufficient.
With only 15 births per day, random variation is large relative to sample size, making days exceeding 60% boys far more probable.

review.explanation: Smaller samples have greater relative variability, so extreme proportions occur more often. This is the classic law of small numbers / sampling variability result.
